groups.text: A payment details endpoint makes three calls at once: account, ledger and risk.
In Kotlin, each one is a child coroutine of one coroutineScope.
Every launch and async makes a child job of the scope.
So the work forms a tree, with the request at the top.
At one hundred milliseconds, the ledger call throws an IOException.
Failure goes up.
The ledger child reports the exception to its parent, the scope.
The scope's job is cancelled with that exception, and a cancelled job cancels all of its children.
Account and risk are cancelled, and their finally blocks run.
The scope waits until those children have really stopped.
Then coroutineScope rethrows the IOException to its caller.
So one failure surfaces as one exception, where the work started.
It took about one hundred milliseconds, not the time of the slowest call, and nothing is left running.
That fits a request.
Without the ledger there is no response, so the other two calls would be wasted work.
Now the other direction.
The client hangs up, and the request is cancelled.
Cancellation goes down.
The scope is cancelled, and then every child below it.
It never goes up.
Cancel only the risk child, and its parent is not told.
A child that ends with CancellationException counts as cancelled, not failed, and the scope carries on.
One catch: cancellation reaches a coroutine only at a suspension point.
A child stuck in a C P U loop or a blocking call finishes that first.
So a failure goes up to the parent, and from there down to the siblings.
Cancellation only goes down.
When siblings should survive each other's failures, you ask for a supervisor instead.
